transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-10-21 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Camila Ortiz (Redwood SE), Ravi Shah (Redwood Platform Eng); Alex Kim (AtlasDynamics VP Eng), Maya Patel (AtlasDynamics SRE), Connor Blake (AtlasDynamics ML Eng)

[00:00] Jordan: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, uh we set aside an hour to go deep on tail latency p95 p99, streaming versus non streaming and, uh, basically the knobs we have in Redwood to control that.
[00:12] Alex: Awesome, thanks Jordan, excited. Our main pain is spikes at p99, like, during bursts we'll see 2x to 3x p99 compared to p95 and it kills our SLAs.
[00:24] Camila: Yeah that's common. Can you give a quick profile — average prompt lengths, tokens, and percent streaming?
[00:30] Connor: Sure, typical prompt is 300-800 tokens, about 20% of calls use streaming for token-by-token UI updates; the rest are non-streaming generation with response sizes around 1k tokens. Peak QPS is ~120 requests/s.
[00:45] Maya: And important — all traffic is inside our VPC, cross-AZ, and we prefer private deployment. We also have strict encryption/KMS needs.
[00:55] Jordan: Perfect. Quick agenda: we’ll walk through latency sources: model compute, batch formation, KV cache hits/misses, quantization performance, and then network/hops for VPC. Then mitigation options: dedicated capacity, prefix caching, adaptive batching, streaming tips, kernel selection.
[01:10] Camila: One note, some transcribed logs might have weird names — K-V cache or K V cache — but it's the same prefix/KV cache feature.
[01:18] Alex: Cool. Start with baseline: what does p95 vs p99 look like on Redwood for similar workloads?
[01:24] Camila: For hosted models, we typically see p95 around model mean + batching latency — for a 13B class model, p95 might be 120-160ms per token for non-streaming short requests if cached, p99 can be 400-900ms depending on cold KV cache and cross-AZ network hops or contention in batching.
[01:40] Ravi: Important to call out continuous batching: it groups requests to amortize model start cost but increases tail if a single slow request is batched repeatedly.
[01:50] Connor: So continuous batching could actually exacerbate p99?
[01:53] Camila: It can if not tuned. We use adaptive time windows and max batch sizes — the goal is to batch without amplifying stragglers. For your traffic, with 120 qps, we might use a short batching window (5-10ms) and max batch size tuned to keep latency within SLOs.
[02:10] Maya: What about KV cache warmup? We saw big differences when cache is cold after a deploy.
[02:16] Camila: KV cache warmup is a big driver. If prefix cache is empty, first few requests pay the full attention KV cost per layer; after warmup p95 drops. We recommend either pre-warming with representative traffic or using sticky routing to keep user sessions on warmed hosts.
[02:32] Alex: Sticky routing — does that require dedicated?
[02:35] Ravi: You can do sticky session routing in Dedicated or via our private deployment config; hosted supports session affinity but Dedicated gives more control over pinning workloads to pools so you keep KV hot.
[02:45] [02:45] Jordan: There's also semantic fallback: if a host is overwhelmed we'll route to a slightly smaller model or quantized variant to keep latency bounded.
[02:53] Connor: On quantization — how much latency improvement versus accuracy cost?
[02:57] Camila: For 4-bit quantization (q4), you typically see 20-40% reduction in per-token latency on GPU on some kernels, sometimes more for CPU inference. But there are edge cases where output quality shifts — so we recommend an eval on your prompt set. Also quantization reduces memory pressure which helps batch sizes and throughput.
[03:17] Maya: Are there cases where quantization increases tail?
[03:20] Camila: Only if kernel paths are less optimized and fallback to a slower path — rare on our runtime because it performs kernel selection, but it's possible for very large sequence lengths or new ops. We'll test it.
[03:32] Alex: Streaming vs non-streaming — which path is faster for tail?
[03:36] Camila: Streaming adds overhead for each chunk: network flushes, small-grain kernel calls, and more context switching. For low-latency token-by-token UI it's good, but p99 can be worse than non-streaming because of many small operations. Non-streaming has one big decode pass which sometimes reduces tail. For you, 20% streaming is moderate; we can recommend hybrid: stream the first N tokens then send non-streamed remainder.
[03:58] Connor: Network hops: our infra is in us-east-1 across two AZs, we see occasional cross-AZ spikes — can Redwood be deployed inside our VPC to avoid that?
[04:08] Jordan: Yes, Redwood Private can run inside your VPC or on-prem. That reduces public-network hops. In VPC we still have intra-AZ and cross-AZ hops depending on placement; you can request AZ affinity for low-latency workloads.
[04:19] Maya: What about TLS termination and LB — those add ms as well.
[04:23] Camila: Correct. TLS and load balancers contribute fixed per-request overhead. For high QPS low latency we suggest TLS offload at the edge and keep long-lived GRPC streaming connections where possible to reduce handshake overhead.
[04:36] Alex: Can you walk through an example trace? We sent a sample earlier.
[04:40] Camila: (pulling up notes) Sure — sample trace shows 18ms network, 12ms LB, 6ms request decode, 220ms model compute, then 30ms serialize + post processing. The p99s had an extra 300ms because of KV cache miss and one host hitting GC due to memory pressure.
[04:58] Connor: GC — is that from Python runtime or from runtime memory management?
[05:01] Ravi: In our runtime, memory pressure can come from KV caches and large batch state; GC events most often in the orchestration layer or microservices, not the GPU kernels. We isolate model compute from orchestration but spikes can cascade if host gets overloaded.
[05:15] Maya: So Mitigations recap — prewarm KV, pin sessions, tune batching windows, consider quantized variants for overflow, AZ affinity, TLS offload, and monitoring. Anything else?
[05:27] Camila: Also token-level caching — if you have repeated prefixes, prefix cache drastically reduces compute per token. And adaptive fallback policies: if latency exceeds threshold, route to a smaller model or increase replication.
[05:39] Alex: About monitoring — what traces/logs will you need from us?
[05:43] Jordan: We'll want representative request traces (timestamps at ingress, host start, model start, model end, egress), token counts, and whether request used streaming or not. Also if you can annotate which requests are from same user/session that helps KV analysis.
[05:57] Connor: We'll export that from our side, but how do you ingest?
[06:00] Camila: Send logs as CSV or the benchmark spreadsheet we'll share. We can also accept OpenTelemetry spans; Redwood supports textile or OTel.
[06:10] Alex: On the Dedicated tier — what are the default kernel and compilation behaviors?
[06:15] Ravi: The runtime compiles and selects kernels based on sequence length and model shape. On Dedicated you can pin kernel sets and disable aggressive autotuning if you want deterministic performance. Compilation time is one-off; we do it ahead of traffic where possible.
[06:28] Maya: What about evicting KV when memory pressure happens?
[06:31] Camila: We maintain an LRU with tiers — small high-frequency entries kept hot, low-frequency evicted. But if memory is constrained, eviction can increase misses and you see p99 spikes. So memory sizing for KV is important for session-heavy workloads.
[06:44] [06:44] Jordan: Quick Q from me — do you have hard p95/p99 targets for pilot?
[06:48] Alex: We want p95 < 200ms and p99 < 600ms for non-streamed requests at 120 qps sustained. Streaming p99 < 800ms.
[06:58] Camila: Those are achievable with dedicated pools, tuned batching (5-10ms window), KV prewarm, and AZ affinity. We'll prototype with a small Dedicated pool.
[07:09] Connor: Any gotchas for on-prem?
[07:12] Ravi: On-prem introduces network and hardware variability. Make sure NIC offloads and kernel versions are compatible; GPU driver and CUDA versions can affect kernel performance. Quantization also depends on GPU support. We'll provide a hardware checklist.
[07:25] Maya: Security — KMS, HSM, SOC2 — how do those integrate?
[07:29] Jordan: For Private we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations. We have SOC2 Type II and can provide audit logs for model access. We'll attach our security pack.
[07:38] Alex: What's the effort to spin up a Dedicated pilot?
[07:41] Jordan: We can provision a small Dedicated pool in 5 business days once contract and infra details are sorted; for VPC it's typically 7-10 days because of networking and KMS keys.
[07:51] Maya: Sounds reasonable. For the benchmark we want to see both streaming and non-streaming runs, KV warm and cold, and quantized and unquantized variants.
[07:59] Camila: Agreed — we'll run 3 runs each: cold KV, warm KV, and quantized variant. We'll include per-token breakdown and p95/p99 latencies and raw spans.
[08:12] Alex: Any quick tips we can implement immediately?
[08:15] Camila: If you can increase session stickiness and prewarm common prefixes, you'll see immediate p99 improvements. Also bump the per-host KV memory if possible to avoid evictions.
[08:25] Connor: We'll try sticky routing and prewarm scripts.
[08:28] Jordan: Cool. Anything else?
[08:31] Maya: No, good deep dive. Let's confirm next steps.
